stem:
The diagram shows sunlight reaching a concave mirror. Parallel rays meet at one place on a scrap of paper.

Why does a bright hot spot form on the paper?

options.text: The concave mirror reflects the parallel rays so that they meet at one small point, concentrating the light energy there.
The concave mirror spreads the parallel rays evenly across the paper, so the whole paper warms at once.
Any mirror makes a hot spot on the paper; the concave shape does not matter.
The paper heats first, and that heat then bends the rays toward the bright spot.

teacher.key_rationale: A concave mirror brings parallel sunlight to a focus, so energy gathers at one small point on the paper. Spreading rays drops the focusing condition. Treating every shiny mirror alike over-widens the rule. Putting paper heat before the ray meeting reverses the cause.
teacher.figure_note: Rewrote plane-mirror angle figure into a concave mirror focusing parallel rays onto paper.
